about: A PROJECT-DEFINED EDITORIAL EQUIVALENT, NOT AN EXTERNAL SYLLABUS. NOTHING IN THIS FILE MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO ANY EXAMINING OR LANGUAGE BODY. core/exam-levels.json records for marwadi that no suitable complete external pre-A1-to-C2 ladder has been identified, and this project has found none either: Marwadi may have no external syllabus at all, and this file must not be read as inventing one. AND NOTHING IN IT MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO DELE, THE INSTITUTO CERVANTES OR THE PLAN CURRICULAR ABOUT MARWADI: they published a Spanish syllabus and have said nothing whatever about this language. READ THE THREE CLAIMS APART. (1) THE POINT SET is derived structurally from core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, this project's restatement of the A1 inventories the Instituto Cervantes publishes behind DELE. That is the strongest thing here and all it establishes is a LEVEL: what an A1 candidate must be able to handle, asked as a language-neutral demand rather than as a piece of Spanish grammar. (2) THE MARWADI EXPONENTS are editorial throughout and are this project's judgement and nobody else's. Deciding that Spanish's three article points are answered by the single fact that Marwadi has none, that its four copula-and-attribute points land on one hai, that its politeness demand is answered by the enclitic particle saa rather than by a pronoun, and that eight separate past-tense points collapse into one absence -- all of that is chosen here. (3) THE COVERAGE NUMBER is a measure of the corpus against this list. It is not an exam-readiness claim and cannot become one while every scope dimension is partial. THE REGISTER COLUMN WAS MEASURED, NOT IMPORTED, because exam-levels.json's caveat for marwadi is about the missing ladder and says nothing about register. What the measurement found is that this track's frontmatter is UNUSUALLY INFORMATIVE: 39 of 257 lessons declare something other than neutral across six values, where latin and portuguese are uniformly neutral and had to be read entirely from bodies. THE CAVEAT ITSELF IS STALE, AND IN THE TRACK'S FAVOUR, AND IS RECORDED AS STALE RATHER THAN DEFERRED TO -- it says the mapping does not claim that the current STARTER CHAPTER reaches the destination, and the track now has 257 lessons across 31 chapters, an assessment spec, task shapes and four-skill scored practice. MW-A1-REG-04 records that. The rest of the caveat stands. WHAT THIS TRACK DOES DIFFERENTLY, said here because the numbers below do not show it: every item runs HEAR, then BUILD IN THE SCRIPT, then PERFORM ACROSS FOUR SCORED SKILLS, and the practice lessons re-run cumulative lists that GROW -- family four, seven, ten, twelve; shopping three, five, seven; food three, five, seven. Seven lessons in ten are a second, third or fourth pass over material already introduced. That is an expanding-interval retrieval schedule built into the curriculum shape rather than bolted on, and MW-A1-SAU-04 enumerates it. NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION: no external search for a Marwadi syllabus was performed for this file; code/learning/human-languages/BACKLOG.d records the sourcing question as settled and directs that it not be repeated per track (HL-C287, HL-C290).
source: PROJECT-DEFINED. LEVEL PROXY: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, the DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Its own source is https://cvc.cervantes.es/ensenanza/biblioteca_ele/plan_curricular/niveles/02_gramatica_inventario_a1-a2.htm and the sibling function, notion and orthography inventories. Nothing about Marwadi is attributed to DELE, the Instituto Cervantes or the Plan Curricular. EXAM ENVELOPE: ONE EXISTS AND IT IS PROJECT-DEFINED. Like latin/ and persian/ and unlike italian/ and portuguese/, the marwadi/ track ships assessment-spec.md, assessment.json, task-shapes/ and track.json, so a project-internal contract does bound this file. It is a contract and not evidence. PROFICIENCY BACKBONE: core/exam-levels.json, tracks.marwadi -- exam 'Coding Adventures Marwadi Assessment -- project-defined equivalent', basis 'editorial', mapping 'cefr', with the no-external-ladder caveat that MW-A1-REG-04 records as partly stale. CORPUS EVIDENCE: every probe was checked mechanically against the atoms declared by the 312 lesson files in code/learning/human-languages/marwadi/lessons/, which introduce 272 distinct atoms between them -- 140 SCRIPT, 90 LEX, 30 PERFORMANCE, 3 DIALOGUE, and single-figure counts of ANSWER, QUESTION, COURTESY, FAREWELL, PHRASE, REGISTER and RESPONSE. All 312 declare variety: central-marwari-devanagari; track.json expands that to contemporary central Marwari in Devanagari, with regional variation named explicitly. NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION: no external search for a Marwadi content syllabus was performed for this file. See `about`.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json
anchors.note: This project's restatement of the A1 inventories the Instituto Cervantes publishes behind DELE. The only inventory in this repository that restates a real awarding body's published syllabus, so it is the only one that can lend a LEVEL. It lends a level and never a language: nothing about Marwadi is attributable to DELE, the Instituto Cervantes or the Plan Curricular.

anchors.title: Council of Europe, CEFR Companion Volume (2020), A1 descriptors
anchors.note: Public, third-party and language-neutral. It can anchor a can-do -- can handle a simple transaction, can indicate when he/she is not following -- and it can never anchor a Marwadi form, because it names none. Used here only where a point is a can-do rather than a structure.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/marwadi/ -- 257 lessons across 31 chapters, curriculum.d and chapters.d
anchors.note: Our own work. It is what every probe resolves against and it is finite and auditable, but agreeing with it is not corroboration: the corpus cannot tell you what an exam would ask, only what this course happens to teach. Where a point's note says a word is missing, that absence was read out of this directory.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/marwadi/assessment-spec.md, assessment.json, task-shapes/ and track.json
anchors.note: The project-internal contract for this track. It bounds what this file may claim and it is not external evidence. track.json is also where the variety claim comes from: contemporary central Marwari in Devanagari, with regional variation named explicitly.

anchors.title: This project's unaided judgement about Marwadi
anchors.note: Every Marwadi exponent below, and every judgement about what counts. Deciding that saa answers the proxy's politeness demand, that the five imperatives cover giving an instruction while the absence of any conjugated lexical verb leaves the present tense empty, and that a market curriculum with no numerals is the headline of this file -- all of that is chosen here. It is a working default to be corrected, not a standard.

proxy.note: EMPTY. Every one of the 273 Spanish points names a demand a Marwadi A1 learner also faces, including the ones that look Spanish-only: the three article points become the single fact that Marwadi has none (MW-A1-ART-01); the preposition-plus-article contraction becomes the postposition (MW-A1-ART-02); the written-accent points become the matra system, where length is carried by a different sign rather than by a mark on the same one (MW-A1-LIP-11); the capital-letter points become the fact that Devanagari has no case distinction at all, which a learner arriving from a Latin-alphabet language needs told (MW-A1-LIP-09); and the nine punctuation points become the danda, which every sentence in this corpus uses and no lesson names (MW-A1-LIP-10). RESTATING A POINT AROUND THE TARGET LANGUAGE'S MACHINERY IS DERIVING IT, not dropping it, and an empty list here is that rule carried to its end rather than a walk that was not done. Unlike Latin, this track has no chronological reason to drop anything either: it teaches a contemporary spoken variety, so the telephone and the internet are ordinary uncovered points rather than anachronisms.

communicative-functions.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's 54 A1 function points) and the Council of Europe CEFR Companion Volume A1 descriptors
communicative-functions.note: The proxy's functional column is finite and level-split, which is what would close a dimension -- for Spanish. It does not close this one, because the exponent that realises each function in Marwadi is our choice every time. Two functions are enumerated that the proxy has no A1 slot for and this track demands anyway: saying that you have understood and that you have not (MW-A1-F2-15, empty), and softening an imperative (MW-A1-V-08, covered). The column's most useful finding is asymmetric: this track can accept, agree, comply and thank, and cannot decline, refuse or disagree at all, because it has no negator.

grammar.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's grammar, sentence and coordination columns)
grammar.note: Walking the Spanish grammar column surfaced demands no reading of the Marwadi corpus alone would have named: that no lexical verb is ever conjugated for a person, that nothing in 257 files is plural, that the word order is verb-final on every page and never named, and that a negator does not exist. It does not close, because Marwadi makes demands Spanish cannot see -- the postposition, the aspirated/unaspirated and retroflex/dental contrasts, the enclitic respect particle -- and those are enumerated here on the project's judgement and, where the proxy has no slot at all, marked marwadiSpecific.

phonology-orthography.source: The Devanagari block of Unicode for the sign inventory, code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json for the orthographic demands, and marwadi/pronunciation-reference.md
phonology-orthography.note: THE DIMENSION THIS TRACK IS STRONGEST IN AND THE PROXY IS WEAKEST FOR. Spanish's orthography column is about an alphabet the learner already has; Marwadi's demand is a different writing system, and the track meets most of it -- 27 consonant signs, all nine dependent vowel signs, the virama, the anusvara and the nukta, each isolated in the chapter where the first word needing it arrives. Two gaps are sharp and specific: only TWO of eleven independent vowel signs exist, so a word beginning with any other vowel cannot be written (aap is drilled from chapter 7 and is unwritable), and neither the Devanagari digits nor the danda is taught at all.

lexicon.source: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json (the proxy's general and specific notion inventories)
lexicon.note: Walked at the granularity of the proxy's numbered subsections. It does not close: which Marwadi words an A1 candidate must hold is what a syllabus would say and there is none. What it does show is a corpus organised entirely around one scenario -- the market counter -- and unusually complete inside it: twelve kinship words, seven shopping words, five transport words, six weather words, six foods, four price words. Outside it there is almost nothing: no numeral, no colour, no part of the day, no body part but the hand, no school word, no work word and no art word.

probeSemantics: A point counts as COVERED when every atom in `probe` is introduced by some lesson in the track. `probe: null` means no atom in the corpus corresponds to this point, which is itself the finding -- an unmapped point is uncovered, never skipped, and its note is written as a work queue. Every atom named in every probe was checked mechanically against the 228 atoms the marwadi track actually introduces; a probe naming an atom that does not exist would report 'not covered' forever and be indistinguishable from real debt, so an id was never invented to fill a point. TWO HABITS ARE NAMED SO THEY ARE NOT HIDDEN GENEROSITIES. First, this track splits one word across several atoms by SKILL: paani has a LEX atom on the lesson that hears it and a SCRIPT atom on the lesson that writes it, and a PERFORMANCE atom on the lesson that scores both. Probing a vocabulary point therefore names the LEX atom and probing a script point names the SCRIPT one; they are the same word reached by two doors, and no point is counted twice for it. Second, this track carries whole PHRASES on single LEX atoms -- MW-LEX-PRICE-QUESTION-01 is the entire sentence ye kitne ku hai?. So a covered functional point often means the learner has a memorised utterance rather than a productive pattern, and the notes say so wherever it matters; MW-A1-ART-02 and MW-A1-V-06 are the clearest cases. A POINT IS NOT COUNTED AS COVERED WHEN ONLY PART OF WHAT IT NAMES IS TAUGHT: haan without a word for no leaves polarity uncovered; ye without vo leaves the far demonstrative uncovered; mhaaro without mhaari leaves possessive agreement uncovered; kaiso without kathe leaves the interrogative adverbs uncovered. `derivedFrom` records each point's provenance -- the proxy point ids whose demand it answers, or an empty list with `marwadiSpecific: true`. `anchorIds` records which anchor each point leans on, and the anchor's `kind` says whether that was something read or something decided. Neither field is read by any code; both are carried so the derivation can be audited rather than trusted.

points.label: proper nouns: a personal name, given and asked for
points.note: Raam, which the track meets first inside the greeting raam-raam saa and then reuses as the name in the exchange.

points.label: place names
points.note: Not one settlement, region or country name in 257 files. Jodhpur, Marwar, Rajasthan: none of them, in a course about the language of that region.

points.label: common nouns naming periods of time
points.note: din, raat, subah, saanjh: ZERO occurrences between them. The track teaches six weather words and no word for a part of the day, so a learner can say it is hot and cannot say when.

points.label: gender: masculine and feminine, and the -o/-i ending that shows it
points.note: Taught IMPLICITLY and well: mhaaro is glossed 'my, agreeing with a masculine noun' the first time it appears, and dada/dadi, nana/nani, sasto/sasti-shaped pairs put the -o/-i contrast in front of the learner repeatedly. No lesson states the rule; the gloss on mhaaro is the closest, and it is enough to count this covered because the point asks that gender be marked and shown.

points.label: gender by heteronymy: the paired kinship words
points.note: maa/baap and bhai/bahan, chapter 8.

points.label: number: the plural
points.note: No plural anywhere. Twelve kinship words, seven food words and seven shopping words are taught and every one of them is singular. A learner at a stall cannot ask for two of anything -- which, given that this track has no numerals either (MW-A1-Q-01), is the same hole seen twice.

points.label: the adjective used predicatively
points.note: ye ghano mahango hai -- this is very expensive. A full predicative sentence with a degree word in it, and the track builds it in chapter 28 out of parts the learner already writes. Several tracks in this series never predicate an adjective of anything at all.

points.label: the adjective used attributively, before its noun
points.note: sasto kapda, ghano paisa: never. Every adjective in the corpus stands in a predicate.

points.label: adjective gender agreement: sasto against sasti
points.note: sasta and mahango are taught in one form each and never varied, so the agreement the noun lessons show on kinship pairs is never carried onto an adjective.

points.label: adjective number agreement
points.note: Behind MW-A1-N-06: there are no plurals to agree with.

points.label: relational adjectives: the gentilic
points.note: Marwari, Rajasthani: absent, and so is any place to be from.

points.label: degree: ghano and thodu
points.note: ghano (very) and thodu (a little), chapter 28, and both are taught in use -- ghano intensifying an adjective and thodu softening a request. This is one of the few tracks in the series that has a degree word at all.

points.label: Marwadi has no article, and a learner must supply one
points.note: Three proxy points collapse into one fact, and the fact is never stated. kapda is cloth, the cloth or a cloth. ye supplies the pointing job an article sometimes does (MW-A1-DEM-01) and nothing supplies the rest.

points.label: the postposition, which is what Marwadi has instead of a preposition-plus-article
points.note: ye kitne ku hai? -- the ku is a postposition, and it is the only one in the corpus. Restated rather than dropped: the Spanish point is about a preposition fusing with an article, and the Marwadi demand behind it is the postposition system. The word is on the page inside a whole-learned question and no lesson names it, so this is COVERED at the level of the phrase and not at the level of the system; see the note on MW-A1-N-06 for the same shape.

points.label: the near demonstrative: ye
points.note: COVERED, WHICH IS RARE IN THIS SERIES. Chapter 26 gives ye its own lesson, glossed as the word that points at one thing in front of you, and then runs it over a shopping word, a food word and a transport word. Bengali, Italian and Latin all report an empty demonstrative column; this track has one and uses it on the day it arrives.

points.label: the far demonstrative: vo
points.note: vo returns ZERO occurrences as a demonstrative in 257 files (the seven raw matches are the -vo ending of dikhavo and lavo). Marwadi's deixis is two-way and the track teaches the near half. Half a system.

points.label: the demonstrative agreeing with what it points at, and standing alone
points.note: ye is used only attributively, in front of a noun, and never alone as this or as these. Its own gender and number forms are never given.

points.label: possessives for one possessor: mhaaro, thaaro
points.note: COVERED, AND EARLY. Chapter 5 teaches both, each glossed as agreeing with a masculine noun, and puts them straight into the name exchange. Latin and Italian both report an empty possessive column.

points.label: possessives for several possessors
points.note: mhaare and thaare, the plural possessors, are absent.

points.label: the possessive agreeing in gender: mhaaro against mhaari
points.note: Both possessives are taught in the masculine only, and the gloss says so, so the learner knows an agreement exists and has never seen the other half. mhaari is unsayable although mhaaro is drilled for twenty chapters.

points.label: cardinal numerals
points.note: CLOSED BY HL-C350, AND THE NOTE IT REPLACED IS WORTH KEEPING IN VIEW: this file's headline used to be that a curriculum whose chapters 26-31 are a market -- how much is this?, how much altogether?, this is very expensive, make it a little cheaper, what final price will you give?, take the money -- taught NO NUMBER AT ALL, and that ek, do, teen, chaar and paanch returned zero across 257 files. Chapters 32-36 teach twelve cardinals: ek, do, teen, chaar, paanch, chha, saat, aath, no, das, bees, so. Each is heard, then written, then scored in four skills, and each has both a LEX and a SCRIPT atom, so the probe names twenty-four word atoms and the two counting payoffs. WHAT IT COST THE HAND: one letter. Every sign in all twelve words was already in the track except independent ए, isolated in MW-W32-e against the े matra it had been writing since chapter 9. That is why this point was affordable and why no per-track reading found it -- the block was never the script. NOT CLOSED, DELIBERATELY: the numbers between ten and twenty. Marwari builds nineteen as ughanis, one short of twenty (the comparative dictionary records ekuncalis, one short of forty, for thirty-nine), so twenty is taught FIRST and the teens wait on four independent vowels and one consonant the track has never taught -- इ for igyaara, अ for atharaa, उ for ughanis, and ळ for solaa. Those are five script lessons, not a numeral gap, and MW-A1-LIP-13 is where they belong.

points.label: ordinal numerals
points.note: STILL ABSENT, and the reason is worth recording because it is NOT the reason it looks like. Marwari's first four ordinals -- pahlo, dujo, tijo, chautho -- need no sign this track has not taught: प ह ल ो, द ू ज ो, त ी ज ो and च ौ थ ो are all in the corpus already, so this is not a script debt and would cost the hand nothing. It was left uncovered by HL-C350 because no citable Marwari-specific source for the ordinal series was found: the Rajasthani numeral list this track cites for the cardinals prints no ordinals, and the comparative dictionary is a cognate list rather than a paradigm. Ordinals are the weakest column in the whole corpus -- twenty tracks enumerate one and eighteen leave it uncovered -- so this is a shared gap, and here it is a SOURCING gap rather than a teaching one. aakhri (final, last) is taught in chapter 29 and remains the only ordering word in the corpus.

points.label: quantifiers: ghano and thodu as quantities rather than degrees
points.note: Both are taught, and taught as degree words on an adjective and a verb rather than as quantifiers on a noun. Counted covered because they ARE the words this notion is built on and the corpus teaches them in use.

points.label: enough
points.note: bas in its enough sense is absent; bas is taught in chapter 21 and it is the bus.

points.label: subject pronouns: hoon, and the polite aap
points.note: hoon (I) in the wellbeing answer and aap (you, polite) in the wellbeing question, chapters 7 and 8. thane, the familiar you, and vo, he or she, are both absent, so the paradigm is two cells of six.

points.label: the familiar second person, against the polite one
points.note: aap is taught and thu / thane are not, so the learner has the polite form only. That is defensible for a market course and it means the tu/vos contrast the register column depends on cannot actually be made with a PRONOUN; see MW-A1-REG-01, where the track carries it on a particle instead.

points.label: object pronouns
points.note: Absent. paisa le lo names the money; there is no way to say give it to me.

points.label: the indirect object, and the experiencer
points.note: Marwadi, like its Indic siblings, puts an experiencer in an oblique case with a postposition. Absent; no lesson has anybody feel, like, need or want anything.

points.label: the reflexive: aapno
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the relative pronoun: jo
points.note: Absent.

points.label: interrogative pronouns: kain and kitno
points.note: kain (what) in chapter 6 and kitno (how much) in chapter 27, each given its own lesson before the question that uses it. kun (who) is absent.

points.label: the exclamative
points.note: Absent, although ghano would build one.

points.label: pronouns with a postposition
points.note: Absent; see MW-A1-PRON-03.

points.label: place deictics: here and there
points.note: Absent. Five places are taught (market, home, temple, shop, stall) and there is no way to say that anything is at one.

points.label: time deictics: aaj, kaal
points.note: Both ZERO occurrences. pachhe (later) is taught in chapter 9 and is the only time adverb in the corpus, and it arrives welded into the farewell pachhe milsoo.

points.label: quantity adverbs
points.note: ghano and thodu are counted at MW-A1-Q-03 and MW-A1-ADJ-06 as degree words; there is no more, no less, and nothing to compare.

points.label: manner adverbs: thik, and its opposite
points.note: thik (fine) is taught inside the wellbeing answer and there is no word for badly, so the health scale has one point on it.

points.label: polarity: haan and its opposite
points.note: haan saa is taught in chapter 3 and given a four-skill performance lesson of its own -- and NO WORD FOR NO EXISTS IN THIS TRACK. koni, nain and naa all return zero occurrences in 257 files (the eight raw matches for naa are inside naana and naani). A learner who is shown the wrong cloth, offered the wrong price or asked a question they must decline has been given the affirmative answer and nothing else. Checked separately from coverage, as this series requires.

points.label: connective adverbs: also, neither
points.note: Absent.

points.label: interrogative adverbs: kaiso, and where
points.note: kaiso (how) is taught in chapter 7, inside the wellbeing question, and kathe (where) is absent. Half a point, and the missing half is what a market course needs most.

points.label: asking why, and answering it
points.note: kyun and kyunki are both absent; see MW-A1-CJ-06.

points.label: the present copula: hai and hoon
points.note: hai closing the name statement (chapter 5) and hoon in the wellbeing answer (chapter 8). Two persons of one verb, and they are the two an introduction needs.

points.label: the present tense of a full verb, in any person
points.note: There is not one. Every verb in the corpus is an IMPERATIVE (MW-A1-V-04) or the copula. A learner cannot say I go, I want, I have, I eat or I understand -- no lexical verb is ever conjugated for a person at all, which is the single largest structural gap in this file.

points.label: the present's values
points.note: Unreachable while MW-A1-V-02 is empty.

points.label: the imperative, and the -o ending every asking word shares
points.note: COVERED, AND WITH FIVE EXPONENTS: dikhavo (show it), karo (make it), lo (take it), do (give), lavo (bring it). Chapter 30 lists them together and matches each to the counter it belongs at, and the lavo lesson names the shared -o ending as the mark of an asking word. Italian's inventory reports no imperative at all; this track has a paradigm-shaped set of them.

points.label: the past
points.note: EIGHT PROXY POINTS, ONE ABSENCE. hua appears once, inside the whole-learned question ye kitno hua?, and is never taken apart. Nothing in 257 files reports anything that has already happened.

points.label: the future
points.note: milsoo (we will meet) in chapter 9 and doge (you will give) inside the final-price question in chapter 29. Both arrive inside whole phrases and neither is named as a future, so this is covered as VOCABULARY and not as a tense; the label says what is actually there. Marked against the proxy's gerund point because the PCIC A1 column has no future slot and this is the nearest non-finite/other-form neighbour.

points.label: the infinitive, and the form a dictionary lists
points.note: No verb in the corpus is ever cited in a base form. Every one arrives as a fixed imperative, which means a learner cannot look one up.

points.label: asking somebody to do something, softened
points.note: thodu sasto karo -- make it a LITTLE cheaper. The softener is taught as a softener, in the lesson that needs it, and chapter 28 says in as many words that it is what keeps a counter-offer polite. The proxy has no A1 slot for softening an imperative and any market conversation needs it.

points.label: the affirmative declarative
points.note: mhaaro naam Raam hai, hoon thik hoon, ye ghano mahango hai. Three sentence patterns, each built from parts the learner writes.

points.label: the negative declarative
points.note: There is no negator in this track at all (MW-A1-ADV-05), so nothing can be denied, refused or corrected. This and MW-A1-Q-01 are the two gaps that most limit what the market scenario can actually do.

points.label: yes-or-no questions
points.note: Every question in the corpus takes an asking word. No polar question is asked anywhere, so haan saa -- which chapter 3 teaches and drills across four skills -- is an answer to a question the track never models.

points.label: questions with an asking word
points.note: thaaro naam kain hai?, aap kaiso ho?, ye kitne ku hai?, kitno aakhri bhaav doge?. Four, and each is heard whole before it is read and written.

points.label: there is, there are
points.note: Absent. hai is a copula here and never an existential, so a learner cannot say the shop has one or there is no water.

points.label: copular and attributive sentences
points.note: FOUR PROXY POINTS ON ONE PATTERN. Marwadi has one copula where Spanish has ser and estar, so the ser/estar split, the attribute and its agreement, and the general-quality notion all land on ye ghano mahango hai and mhaaro naam Raam hai.

points.label: transitive sentences, and the object of a request
points.note: ye kapda dikhavo and chaay lavo -- an object in front of its verb, which is where Marwadi puts it and where Spanish does not. The word order is never named as word order.

points.label: word order: Marwadi is subject-object-verb
points.note: Every sentence in the corpus is verb-final and no lesson says so. A learner coming from English or Spanish has been shown the pattern twenty times and never told it is a pattern.

points.label: agreement inside the phrase, and between subject and verb
points.note: mhaaro is glossed as agreeing with a masculine noun and no lesson ever states an agreement rule or varies a form to show one; see MW-A1-ADJ-03 and MW-A1-POS-03.

points.label: the vocative
points.note: Nobody is ever addressed by name. saa does the respect job a vocative often carries (MW-A1-REG-01) and is not a vocative.

points.label: copulative coordination: ar
points.note: THE JOINING COLUMN IS FLAT ZERO, WHICH MAKES IT THE ELEVENTH TRACK IN THIS SERIES TO REPORT ONE. ar (the Marwadi and), ane and Hindi's aur all return ZERO occurrences in 257 files. A learner who has twelve kinship words, seven foods and seven shopping words cannot say bread and tea.

points.label: negative coordination: neither, nor
points.note: Unreachable: there is no negator (MW-A1-ADV-05).

points.label: disjunctive coordination: ya
points.note: Zero occurrences, and it is the word a stall conversation needs most after the numbers: this one or that one.

points.label: adversative coordination: pan
points.note: pan and par both return ZERO occurrences. The bargaining exchange in chapter 31 runs five turns and never once sets one against another.

points.label: distributive coordination
points.note: Absent.

points.label: causal clauses: kyunki
points.note: Zero. A learner can say this is very expensive and cannot say why anything is anything.

points.label: the complement clause: ke
points.note: ke returns ZERO occurrences in 257 files.

points.label: the relative clause
points.note: Marwadi's jo ... vo correlative is absent in both halves.

points.label: the infinitive clause, as subject and as object
points.note: Behind MW-A1-V-07: no verb in the corpus has a base form to put in a clause.

points.label: purpose clauses
points.note: Absent.

points.label: simultaneity: jad
points.note: Zero.

points.label: ask for information about a person or a thing
points.note: thaaro naam kain hai? for the person and ye kitne ku hai? for the thing. Two, and the second is the one the whole curriculum is built toward.

points.label: give personal information: name
points.note: The name is the whole of it. Age is unsayable because there are no numbers (MW-A1-Q-01), and origin because there are no place names (MW-A1-N-02), so the identity slot has one of its three fields.

points.label: ask for confirmation with a tag
points.note: Absent.

points.label: confirm or deny the previous statement
points.note: haan saa confirms, and there is nothing to deny with (MW-A1-ADV-05). Half a point, and the missing half is the half a bargain needs.

points.label: ask for an opinion by handing the turn back
points.note: Absent; the exchanges are all question-and-answer with a fixed asker.

points.label: give an opinion
points.note: No verb of thinking or saying exists in the corpus.

points.label: ask for an evaluation
points.note: aap kaiso ho?. It asks after a person rather than a thing, which is what this level uses it for.

points.label: evaluate
points.note: thik is the only evaluation word and its opposite is absent (MW-A1-ADV-04), so the scale has one point on it and a candidate asked how something was cannot say badly.

points.label: express approval and disapproval
points.note: ye ghano mahango hai is a disapproval, and it is taught as one -- chapter 28 calls it the reply that starts a bargain. Approval has no exponent, so this is covered on the negative side only; the label says evaluate rather than approve for that reason.

points.label: express agreement
points.note: haan saa, and chapter 3 gives it a four-skill performance lesson, which is more weight than most tracks put on a one-word answer.

points.label: express disagreement
points.note: Unreachable without a negator.

points.label: show scepticism
points.note: Absent.

points.label: offer a counter-argument
points.note: thodu sasto karo is a counter-move and it is a request rather than an argument, because pan (but) is absent (MW-A1-CJ-04). Counted covered because at A1 the counter-offer IS the counter-argument in a market.

points.label: express possibility
points.note: Absent.

points.label: ask whether somebody knows something
points.note: Absent.

points.label: express knowledge, and ignorance
points.note: No verb of knowing or thinking anywhere in 257 files. Three proxy points and one absence.

points.label: ask about ability, and express it
points.note: Absent.

points.label: say that you have understood, and that you have not
points.note: THE REPAIR COLUMN, CHECKED SEPARATELY, AND THERE IS NOTHING. No verb of understanding, no word for again, no way to negate. samajh, phir and dhire all return zero occurrences. A learner standing at the counter this course is built around, who mishears the price, has been given no move at all -- and the price is the one thing they most need to hear correctly. The proxy has no A1 slot for this and CEFR's A1 descriptors do.

points.label: express likes
points.note: No experiencer construction and no verb of liking. Seven food words and no way to say you like any of them.

points.label: ask about a preference by offering alternatives
points.note: Needs ya; see MW-A1-CJ-03.

points.label: express a preference
points.note: Absent.

points.label: express a wish or a want
points.note: chaahiye, the one word that would let a learner ask for a thing without an imperative, is absent. The track asks for things by commanding instead, which works at a stall and nowhere else.

points.label: ask about plans
points.note: Absent.

points.label: express a plan or an intention
points.note: pachhe milsoo -- see you later -- is a stated intention to meet, and it is the only one. Thin, and it is what the farewell slot at this level actually contains.

points.label: ask for an object, softened
points.note: ye kapda dikhavo, with thodu available as the softener the bargaining lesson teaches. There is no word for please: kripya and its Marwadi equivalents return zero occurrences, and the register particle saa is what carries politeness instead (MW-A1-REG-01). That is a real Marwadi answer to the demand rather than a gap, which is why this is covered and Italian's equivalent point is not.

points.label: ask for help
points.note: Absent.

points.label: respond to a request
points.note: haan saa, and paisa le lo as the compliance move that closes the purchase.

points.label: grant permission
points.note: Absent.

points.label: refuse permission
points.note: Unreachable without a negator.

points.label: offer and invite
points.note: lo -- take it. Chapter 29 calls it the shortest asking word in the source and it is exactly the offer move a counter uses.

points.label: decline an offer
points.note: Unreachable without a negator. In a bargaining curriculum this is the single most consequential missing move: the learner can open a negotiation and cannot walk away from one.

points.label: greet
points.note: raam-raam saa, chapter 1, with the full exchange in the same chapter.

points.label: respond to a greeting
points.note: raam-raam saa answered with raam-raam saa, raam-raam -- and the second turn drops the particle, which is register teaching (MW-A1-REG-02).

points.label: address somebody by name or title
points.note: No title and no vocative; see MW-A1-OS-10.

points.label: introduce a third person
points.note: Absent, and behind the missing third-person pronoun.

points.label: respond to an introduction
points.note: The name exchange returns the same question rather than acknowledging; there is no pleased-to-meet-you move.

points.label: apologise
points.note: maaf karo would be built from karo, which chapter 28 teaches, and the apology itself is absent.

points.label: thank
points.note: aabhaar, chapter 2, with a lesson on when a formal thanks is the right one. The reply to thanks has no exponent.

points.label: offer condolences
points.note: Absent.

points.label: propose a toast
points.note: Absent.

points.label: congratulate
points.note: Absent.

points.label: take leave
points.note: pachhe milsoo, chapter 9, heard whole and then written.

points.label: greet and respond within a conversation
ask for a person
points.note: Absent.

points.label: show that one is following
points.note: haan saa can be a backchannel and is never presented as one; counted covered because the exponent exists and is drilled, and read the limit with MW-A1-F2-15.

points.label: ask somebody to be quiet
points.note: Absent.

points.label: propose closing the conversation
points.note: paisa le lo closes the transaction and the five-turn counter exchange ends on it.

points.label: presence and absence: with and without
points.note: Absent, and so is any way to locate an event in time or to hedge a claim.

points.label: measures: size, distance and weight
points.note: Absent, and unreachable without numerals. A market course with no kilo and no metre.

points.label: relative position, distance, and direction
points.note: Three proxy points, no exponent between them. The track calls its chapter 10 set direction and travel words and they are place NOUNS -- market, home, temple -- with nothing to relate them by.

points.label: movement and stability
points.note: lavo, bring it, is the only motion in the corpus and it is an imperative. jaavo and aavo, go and come, are both absent.

points.label: order: first, before, after
points.note: aakhri, final -- taught in chapter 29 as the word that ends a bargain. It is the only ordering word and it is exactly the one this curriculum needs.

points.label: origin: where somebody is from
points.note: No place name (MW-A1-N-02), no gentilic (MW-A1-ADJ-05), no postposition for from. Three gaps, one unanswerable question -- and it is the second question anybody is asked.

points.label: the clock and the parts of the day
points.note: Absent; see MW-A1-N-03. Also unreachable without numerals.

points.label: locating in time: today, weekdays, months, seasons
points.note: ZERO of it. Six weather words are taught, including garmi and thandi -- which the lessons note the source also uses for summer and winter -- so the track holds two season senses inside weather words and teaches no season, no month and no day.

points.label: anteriority and posteriority
points.note: pachhe, later. It arrives inside the farewell and the lesson glosses it separately, which is why it counts.

points.label: sight and hearing
points.note: dikhavo, show it, is causative-of-seeing and is the only perception word in the corpus. Hearing has none, which is worth noting in a track whose every vocabulary item is HEARD before it is read.

points.label: colour
points.note: Not one colour word in 257 files -- and the track teaches seven clothing and shopping words, where the first question at a cloth stall is which colour.

points.label: age
points.note: Unreachable without numerals.

points.label: open and closed, way in and way out
points.note: Absent, and a shop that cannot be open or closed is a gap this curriculum will feel.

points.label: value and price
points.note: bhaav (price), sasta (cheap), mahango (expensive) and the price question itself. THE BEST-COVERED NOTION IN THE FILE, and read it against MW-A1-Q-01: the learner can ask a price, judge it and counter it, and cannot say or understand a number.

points.label: attractiveness, acceptability, correctness, interest, ease
points.note: Five proxy points, no exponent between them. The evaluative vocabulary of this track is entirely about price.

points.label: quality: good and bad
points.note: thik is fine and there is no good and no bad. See MW-A1-F2-04.

points.label: verbal expression: saying, speaking, writing
points.note: No verb of speaking or writing, which is a curious absence in a track that spends 41 lessons teaching the learner to write.

points.label: parts of the body
points.note: haath (hand) is taught in chapter 10 as a travel word and is the ONLY body part in 257 files. One is not the set.

points.label: physical characteristics, and character
points.note: Absent.

points.label: actions and positions of the body
points.note: Absent.

points.label: personal data beyond the name
points.note: No surname, no address, no telephone number, no age. See MW-A1-F1-03.

points.label: documents, and personal objects
points.note: Absent.

points.label: family relationships
points.note: TWELVE, INCLUDING THE PATERNAL/MATERNAL GRANDPARENT SPLIT that Indo-Aryan makes and Spanish does not -- dada/dadi against nana/nani. Chapters 8 and 9, built up four at a time and re-run cumulatively as four, seven, ten and twelve. The densest and best-scheduled block in the track.

points.label: social relationships beyond the family
points.note: dost, the friend, is absent; so are neighbour, colleague and shopkeeper -- the last of which is the person every one of these lessons is talking to.

points.label: celebrations and occasions
points.note: Absent.

points.label: food
points.note: daal, ghee, sabji, roti, baati, churma -- six, and three of them (baati, churma, and daal beside them) are the Rajasthani dish this region is actually known for, which is a curriculum decision worth crediting.

points.label: drink
points.note: paani in chapter 4, the first content word the track teaches, and chaay in chapter 25.

points.label: the meals of the day
points.note: Absent, and behind MW-A1-N-03: no part of the day exists to name a meal after.

points.label: ordering at a stall
points.note: chaay lavo -- bring tea. Chapter 30 says in as many words that this is the request a food counter actually hears.

points.label: school, teaching and learning
points.note: SEVEN PROXY POINTS AND NOT ONE EXPONENT. No school, no teacher, no pupil, no book, no lesson and no classroom language -- which is the more striking because 41 of the 257 lessons are writing lessons: the track teaches handwriting and has no word for it.

points.label: work: professions, workplaces, activity
points.note: SIX PROXY POINTS, NO EXPONENT. dukan (shop) is taught as a place to buy from, never as a place to work in, and the shopkeeper on the other side of every counter in this curriculum has no name.

points.label: free time, games, sport and entertainment
points.note: Four proxy points, no exponent.

points.label: media, correspondence, telephone and internet
points.note: Six proxy points, no exponent.

points.label: the dwelling
points.note: ghar, home, taught in chapter 10 with the places. The parts of a house, the furniture and the domestic activities are all absent -- four proxy points land here and one word answers the first of them.

points.label: services: post, bank, health, security
points.note: Four proxy points, no exponent.

points.label: shopping: the place, the goods and the act
points.note: dukan, vastu, samaan, bajar -- shop, item, goods and market. Chapters 10 and 18 to 20.

points.label: clothing
points.note: kapda, cloth or clothes, chapter 20 -- and it is the noun the show-me request is first run on. One word, and it is the one the curriculum uses.

points.label: payment and money
points.note: paisa (money) and paisa le lo (take the money). Two proxy points on one closing move -- and no amount can be named; see MW-A1-Q-01.

points.label: health, illness, medicine and hygiene
points.note: Four proxy points, no exponent. thik in the wellbeing answer is the nearest and it is about mood.

points.label: travel objects, documents and accommodation
points.note: Absent.

points.label: transport
points.note: bas, gaadi, thela, riksha, ghodo -- FIVE, from the bus to the handcart to the horse, chapters 21 and 22. Better covered than in any other track in this series, and there is no verb of travelling and no fare to pay because there are no numbers.

points.label: commerce, businesses and industry
points.note: Three proxy points, no exponent: the buyer and the seller are never named, though both are in every dialogue.

points.label: computing and new technology
points.note: Absent.

points.label: government, politics, law and justice
points.note: Absent.

points.label: the arts
points.note: SIX PROXY POINTS AND NO EXPONENT, and this is the one to fix first if the track wants a cultural spine: Rajasthan's folk music, its miniature painting and its puppet theatre are all absent, and so is any word for song, dance or story.

points.label: religion
points.note: mandir, the temple, in chapter 10 -- and the greeting itself, raam-raam saa, is a divine name said twice, which the chapter 1 lesson treats as a greeting rather than as religion. Counted covered because the exponent is there and its origin is on the page.

points.label: the universe and the sky
points.note: sooraj, chaand, taaro: absent. Six weather words and no sun.

points.label: country, town and city
points.note: gaon, shahar, desh: absent. bajar (market) is the largest place this track can name.

points.label: urban and rural spaces
points.note: bajar, ghar, mandir -- market, home, temple. Chapter 10's set is three points of a Rajasthani town and it is what this notion asks for at A1.

points.label: climate and weather
points.note: SIX -- wind, cloud, rain, weather, heat and cold, chapters 16 and 17, built three then six. In a desert region this is the right notion to spend two chapters on, and it is uncovered in most of the tracks measured before this one.

points.label: fauna
points.note: ghodo, the horse, taught in chapter 22 as transport. One animal, doing another notion's work.

points.label: flora
points.note: Absent. sabji (vegetables) is a food word.

points.label: the Devanagari consonant signs
points.note: TWENTY-SEVEN consonant signs are taught across the 41 writing lessons, each isolated in the chapter where the first word needing it arrives -- gha with ghar, ja with bajar, dda with thandi, kha with dikhavo. Twenty of them are probed here. Devanagari has 33, so this is 27 of 33 and the six missing are the ones no taught word needs.

points.label: the aspirated / unaspirated consonant pairs
points.note: Six pairs, each half taught, though never explicitly as a pair. The distinctive Indic contrast that a Romance-language proxy has no point for at all, derived here from the consonant-letters point.

points.label: the retroflex / dental contrast
points.note: All three pairs are taught -- and the naming is careful: the retroflex nna arrives in chapter 4 for paani and is later reused, by name, to build ghano.

points.label: the dependent vowel signs (matras)
points.note: NINE, and the short-i matra is taught with its own oddity named: it is written BEFORE the consonant it follows. The vowel column is closed.

points.label: the independent vowel signs
points.note: ONLY TWO EXIST IN THIS TRACK: aa (chapter 2, for aabhaar) and ii (chapter 6). Devanagari has eleven. So a learner can write any vowel INSIDE a word and can begin a word with only two of them -- ek, aap and unnho are unwritable, and aap is a word this track teaches and drills from chapter 7. The nearest miss in the script column.

points.label: the virama, and the conjunct
points.note: The vowel-killer is taught in chapter 5 and then used to build patni and bachcha. The general rule for forming a conjunct is never stated; two worked instances are.

points.label: the anusvara
points.note: The dot above, taught in chapter 3 on haan.

points.label: the nukta
points.note: The dot below, taught in chapter 20 on kapda -- the retroflex flap, which is exactly where a Marwadi learner meets it.

points.label: capital letters, and the absence of case
points.note: Devanagari has no case distinction at all, which is a whole demand the proxy makes and this script cannot meet. Restated rather than dropped, and it is worth a lesson: a learner coming from a Latin-alphabet language will look for capitals at the start of Raam and never find one, and no lesson tells them not to.

points.label: the danda, and Devanagari punctuation
points.note: NINE PROXY POINTS COLLAPSE INTO ONE MARK AND IT IS NEVER TAUGHT. Every declarative sentence in this corpus is written with the danda -- mhaaro naam Raam hai. -- and no lesson names it or says that it is Devanagari's full stop. The question mark and the comma the corpus also uses are borrowed from the Latin tradition, which is also never said.

points.label: written accentuation
points.note: Devanagari writes no accent, and vowel length is carried by a different matra rather than by a mark on the same one. Restated onto the matra system, which MW-A1-LIP-04 reports closed; enumerated separately because the DEMAND -- that a length difference changes a word -- is never stated anywhere, and this track has minimal pairs on the page (thik against theek-shaped spellings, dada against dadi).

points.label: abbreviations, initialisms and symbols
points.note: Four proxy points, no exponent. The rupee sign, which a price question needs, is among them.

points.label: the Devanagari digits
points.note: CLOSED BY HL-C350. Chapter 35 teaches all ten signs, three at a time across four writing lessons, each set cashed immediately against the words it writes. This is a READING gap as much as a counting one -- a price ticket, a fare and a form are written in these shapes and not in words -- so the chapter is built around the four that a Latin-trained eye reads wrongly: ४ is taken for an eight, ५ for a four, ७ for a nine and ८ for a letter. Those four are drilled beside ०, ३, ६ and ९, which a Latin eye guesses correctly, and they close alone in MW-R35-script-close. STILL OPEN in the script column, and named here rather than at MW-A1-Q-01 because they are letters: इ, अ, उ and ळ, which the numbers eleven to nineteen need.

points.label: the saa particle, which is where this language keeps its politeness
points.note: THE FIRST THING THE TRACK TEACHES AND THE RIGHT ONE. saa is an enclitic respect particle: raam-raam saa is the respectful greeting, haan saa the respectful yes. Marwadi carries at A1 on a PARTICLE what Italian carries on a pronoun and Latin does not carry at all -- and this track has no familiar second-person pronoun (MW-A1-PRON-02), so the particle is not merely one option, it is the only register machinery the learner has.

points.label: dropping the particle, and what that means
points.note: Chapter 1's exchange answers raam-raam saa with raam-raam saa, raam-raam -- the particle present on the first return and dropped on the second. That is a register move shown rather than stated, and it is shown on the first page.

points.label: what the frontmatter register field records, against what the lessons teach
points.note: MEASURED, NOT IMPORTED. core/exam-levels.json's caveat for marwadi says nothing about register; it is about the missing external ladder. So this column was read out of lesson bodies and frontmatter directly. The frontmatter here is UNUSUALLY INFORMATIVE compared with the other tracks in this batch: 39 of 257 lessons declare something other than neutral, across six values -- neutral-familiar (13), familiar (12), respectful (6), polite-formal (3), neutral-friendly (3), formal (2) -- and all 257 declare variety: central-marwari-devanagari, which track.json expands to contemporary central Marwari with regional variation named explicitly. Latin and Portuguese, by contrast, are uniformly neutral and their register columns had to be read entirely from bodies.

points.label: THE CAVEAT IN exam-levels.json IS STALE, AND IN THE TRACK'S FAVOUR
points.note: Recorded rather than deferred to, following the precedent of the track whose caveat was found overstated. marwadi's caveat says the project-defined equivalent must test four skills with published task shapes, rubrics, pass thresholds and timed mocks, and that the mapping 'does not claim that the current STARTER CHAPTER reaches it'. The track has 257 lessons across 31 chapters, ships assessment-spec.md, assessment.json and task-shapes/, and its practice lessons are already scored across four separate skills -- 25 PERFORMANCE atoms carry exactly that. The caveat describes a track that no longer exists. The rest of it stands: no external Marwadi pre-A1-to-C2 ladder has been identified, and this file does not claim one.

points.category: Saudo (the counter transaction this track is built around)
points.label: run a five-turn counter exchange end to end
points.note: THE THING THIS TRACK IS FOR, AND THE PROXY HAS NO POINT FOR IT. Chapter 31 runs one five-turn exchange -- show me this cloth / how much is it / that is very expensive / make it a little cheaper / take the money -- at a shop, a food stall and a rickshaw, in four separately scored skills. The PCIC A1 functional inventory enumerates the moves one at a time and never asks a candidate to chain them, and chaining them is what a market actually requires.

points.category: Saudo (the counter transaction this track is built around)
points.label: run the same exchange over a different noun
points.note: Every request lesson is immediately re-run over a shopping word, a food word and a transport word. That is the generalisation step -- the learner is shown that the frame is a frame -- and it happens three times in six chapters.

points.category: Saudo (the counter transaction this track is built around)
points.label: match the asking word to the counter it belongs at
points.note: Chapter 30 lists the five imperatives together and pairs each with its setting: dikhavo at a cloth counter, lavo at a food counter, lo and do across a till. Pragmatic selection between near-synonyms, taught explicitly, at A1.

points.category: Saudo (the counter transaction this track is built around)
points.label: hear a whole utterance before reading it, and write it after
points.note: THE TRACK'S OWN METHOD, AND WHY ITS REINFORCEMENT WINDOWS COME BACK CLEAN. Every item runs the same cycle: a listening-speaking lesson hears it, a word or writing lesson builds it from signs the hand already owns, and a practice-mix lesson performs it across four scored skills. 70 of the 257 lessons are listening-speaking, 41 are writing and 74 are practice-mix, so roughly seven lessons in ten are a second, third or fourth pass over material already introduced -- and the practice lessons re-run cumulative lists that GROW (family four, seven, ten, twelve; shopping three, five, seven; food three, five, seven), which is an expanding-interval retrieval schedule built into the curriculum shape rather than bolted on. No proxy point exists for a teaching method; it is enumerated because it is the reason this track's numbers below are what they are.
